summary: This Standards Track document defines a GeneralName.otherName for the X.509 Subject and Issuer Alternative Name extensions to carry an IEEE MAC address, binding a Layer 2 interface identifier to a certificate's public key. It also defines how Name Constraints apply to it.

eli5.summary: A digital ID card can now include a gadget's hardware address, as in "this key belongs to this exact network gadget".

questions: how to put a mac address in an x509 certificate
how do mac address name constraints work
subtitle: A standard way to put a device's hardware (MAC) address into an X.509 certificate, and to constrain it.

tldr.problem: Deployments that identify a device by its MAC address in an X.509 certificate had no standard encoding in the Subject Alternative Name extension.
tldr.mechanism: A new otherName form, id-on-MACAddress, carries a 6-octet EUI-48 or 8-octet EUI-64 as an OCTET STRING. In Name Constraints the same form carries a value and a mask, so the string is 12 or 16 octets.
tldr.outcome: Certificates can bind a Layer 2 interface identifier to a public key, which helps Layer 2 authentication and secure provisioning in IoT and automotive networks. The binding is only as strong as the CA's checks, and fixed MAC addresses allow tracking.

today: RFC 10031 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Some deployments use X.509 certificates to identify a device by its Media Access Control (MAC) address, but had no standard way to encode it in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension of RFC 5280. RFC 10031 defines a new otherName form called MACAddress. It carries either a 48-bit IEEE 802 MAC address (EUI-48) or a 64-bit extended identifier (EUI-64) in an OCTET STRING.

The same name form can express constraints on EUI-48 or EUI-64 values in the Name Constraints extension (NCE). The RFC says this enables certificate-based authentication at Layer 2 and secure provisioning in Internet of Things (IoT) and automotive networks in particular. The form can also appear in an Issuer Alternative Name (IAN) extension, but the RFC notes there are probably few, if any, reasons to do so.
sections.eli5: A name tag usually shows a name. This RFC lets the tag show a gadget's hardware serial number instead.

sections.title: Encoding a MAC Address as a Name
sections.content:
The name form is identified by the object identifier id-on-MACAddress, 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.8.12. In a SAN or IAN the value is exactly six or eight octets, most significant octet first. No text form is permitted in the certificate. Human-readable forms such as 00-24-98-7B-19-02 are used only in management interfaces.

If a device has a 48-bit MAC identifier, the Certification Authority (CA) MUST encode it as a 6-octet OCTET STRING. If its factory identifier is a 64-bit EUI-64, or no canonical 48-bit form exists, the CA MUST use an 8-octet OCTET STRING. For example, 00-24-98-7B-19-02 encodes as '0024987B1902'H.
sections.eli5: The address is written as plain bytes, not as text with dashes. Dashes are only for people reading a screen.

sections.title: Encoding a MAC Address Constraint
sections.content:
In the Name Constraints extension the OCTET STRING is twice as long as the address type it constrains: 12 octets for EUI-48 and 16 for EUI-64. It holds two parts of N octets each, where N is 6 or 8. The first part is the value bit pattern, which the masked address must contain to match. The second is the mask bit pattern. Each bit set in the mask means the same bit position in the address is constrained by the value.

For example, a constraint for the OUI 00-00-5e uses value '00005E000000'H and a mask with the first three octets set, giving the OCTET STRING '00005E000000FFFFFF000000'H. Bits are encoded most significant first.

If a bit is not set in the mask, the CA MUST NOT set the matching bit in the value. This gives one canonical encoding for each constraint. As RFC 5280 says, an NCE MUST be used only in a CA certificate.
sections.eli5: A rule says which bytes of the address to look at (the mask) and what they must equal (the value). Everything else is allowed.

sections.title: Generation and Validation Rules
sections.content:
The CA MUST ensure that MACAddress names in certificates it issues are owned, or expected to be owned, by the subject device for the certificate's lifetime. The same MAC address MUST NOT appear in certificates for different devices, unless they share the same Layer 2 interface.

A relying party matching a presented MAC address to a certificate SHALL compare the OCTET STRING contents byte for byte. Wildcards are not supported. A self-signed certificate with a MACAddress name MUST include the address of one of the device's physical ports.
sections.eli5: Two different gadgets must not wear the same serial-number tag, and the tag must really belong to the gadget wearing it.

sections.title: Name Constraint Matching and Path Processing
sections.content:
An NCE MAY impose permittedSubtrees and excludedSubtrees on names of type id-on-MACAddress. To test a name against a constraint, an application first rejects a length mismatch: a 6-octet name never matches a 16-octet constraint, and an 8-octet name never matches a 12-octet constraint. It then XORs the name with the value part and ANDs the result with the mask part. The name matches only if every bit of the result is zero. Implementations need not use this algorithm, but MUST get identical results.

For example, the constraint '000000000000 030000000000'H matches any universal, unicast EUI-48 address such as 00-00-5e-00-50-34.

For certification path validation, the RFC specifies how to extend the procedures of RFC 5280. Initial permitted subtrees accept all EUI-48 and all EUI-64 addresses, and initial excluded subtrees are empty. Permitted subtrees are intersected down the path: a new constraint is kept only if it is a subset of a constraint from the previous level, meaning it has the same length, adds mask bits without removing any, and keeps the values of the parent's live bits. Excluded subtrees are the union of all constraints. The RFC warns that nested NCEs can end up prohibiting all names even when that was not intended.
sections.eli5: To check a name, ignore the bytes the rule does not care about and see whether the rest match exactly. Each CA below can only make the rules stricter, never looser.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The binding of a MAC address to a certificate is only as strong as the CA's validation. CAs MUST verify that the subscriber legitimately controls or owns the address, and the validation MUST account for MAC address spoofing. Dynamically assigned or shared addresses can undermine the uniqueness and accountability this name form aims to provide. Unlike IP addresses, MAC addresses are not typically routed across Layer 3 boundaries, so relying parties SHOULD NOT assume uniqueness beyond their local network without information that addresses are stable across boundaries.

On the privacy side, a MAC address can uniquely identify a physical device and, by extension, its user. Certificates that embed unchanging addresses make long-term tracking easier. Deployments SHOULD consider rotating addresses, short-lived certificates or MAC address randomization where feasible.

Flag bits in the first octet let implementations exclude multicast and local addresses, but they cannot prove a 24-bit value is an IEEE-registered OUI. CAs MUST include only addresses the subscriber legitimately controls, for example after consulting the IEEE registry.
sections.eli5: A serial number on a tag proves little if anyone can copy it. The tag-maker has to check, and a never-changing number lets people follow a gadget around.

sections.title: Registrations and Examples
sections.content:
IANA assigned decimal 126, id-mod-mac-address-other-name-2025, in the "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" registry, and decimal 12, id-on-MACAddress, in the "SMI Security for PKIX Other Name Forms" registry. The ASN.1 module defines MACAddress ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE (6 | 8 | 12 | 16)).

The examples show an EUI-48 name '0024987B1902'H, an EUI-64 name 'ACDE480011223344'H, and a constraint '000000000000 030000000000'H that allows only universal, unicast EUI-48 values. The constraint uses the Individual/Group bit (0 is unicast) and the Universal/Local bit (0 is universal).
sections.eli5: The RFC also adds new entries to the official lists of names and shows sample tags you can copy.
